title: Document Image Verification Based on Paragraph Alignment and Subtle Change Detection
research_question: Can document images be verified against stored references by combining paragraph-structure retrieval, geometric paragraph alignment, and contrastive visual comparison robust to print-scan distortions and subtle content changes?
methodology: The system first segments paragraphs with Faster R-CNN and represents each reference document through structural descriptors including paragraph count, bounding boxes, normalized areas, aspect ratios, and neighboring-paragraph relationships; a four-step matching procedure retrieves candidate references and establishes paragraph correspondences. Matched input paragraphs are geometrically aligned to their reference counterparts, divided into smaller blocks, and compared using a contrastively trained ResNet50 feature extractor, followed by an additional neighborhood-based verification step intended to reject residual misalignment false positives. Experiments use a PubLayNet-derived retrieval database and a second English/Chinese print-scan and tampering database, with retrieval benchmarks, change-detection baselines, and ablations.

key_findings.finding: The proposed structural retrieval method achieved 0.976 precision, 0.96 hit rate, 24.29 ms average retrieval time, and a 1.33 MB retrieval data size in the reported Database A experiment.

With paragraph alignment, the final verification scheme achieved 0.949 precision, 0.978 recall, 0.963 accuracy, and 0.963 F1; removing paragraph alignment reduced precision to 0.725, accuracy to 0.788, and F1 to 0.814 while recall remained 0.975.
At threshold 0.9, adding the secondary verification step increased precision from 0.767 to 0.949 and accuracy from 0.840 to 0.963 while recall remained 0.978.
VGG19 produced a higher precision of 0.976, but the proposed aligned method had substantially higher recall and a higher F1 score, 0.978 and 0.963 versus 0.910 and 0.942.
The approach establishes paragraph-level correspondences independently of OCR text and was evaluated with English and Chinese documents as well as changes affecting text, images, and tables.
Removing position matching from the four-step retrieval procedure reduced retrieval precision from 0.976 to 0.886 while leaving the reported hit rate at 0.96.

limitations: Performance depends on accurate paragraph segmentation, which can be difficult for documents with highly variable or uncommon content types.
The comparison remains sensitive to feature mismatch caused by geometric distortion.
Rotation of the input document relative to its reference can degrade detection performance.
The paper's constructed datasets are not readily available because the authors state that the data are part of an ongoing study.

The system compares an input document against candidate reference images and detects changed content, but it does not evaluate longitudinal multi-version lineage or provenance graphs across a sequence of revisions.
raw_claims: The verification pipeline has a reference-retrieval stage followed by a content-change-detection stage.
Paragraph structure rather than recognized text is used to retrieve candidate reference document images.
The structural descriptor includes paragraph geometry and neighborhood information.
The retrieval procedure also establishes paragraph correspondences between the input and candidate references.
Paragraph alignment is performed before fine-grained block comparison.
A contrastively trained ResNet50 representation is used to distinguish genuine and changed blocks under print-scan distortions.
A second verification pass examines neighboring regions to reduce false positives caused by residual misalignment.
Database A includes 20,000 reference document images selected from PubLayNet for retrieval testing.
Database B contains English and Chinese documents and includes print-scan and deliberately modified samples.
The final aligned configuration reports 0.963 accuracy and 0.963 F1.
The authors report that paragraph alignment is important for avoiding false modification detections caused by spatial mismatch.
The study's constructed datasets are not presently released because they are part of ongoing work.
